# 2. The Sharing–Sparing Axis {#sec-sharing-sparing}

### 2.1 The positions {#sec-positions}

The second dimension, independent of [scale](1-the-scale-transect.qmd). Does the array **share** land with agricultural production, **spare** land by taking ground out of it — or neither?

This borrows the land-sharing / land-sparing framing from conservation ecology, where the debate is authentically unsettled — which is precisely why it makes a good axis. It describes a real choice without ranking the options.

| Position | Description | Characteristic |
|---|---|---|
| **S1 — Full sharing** | Production continues within the array footprint, in the same ground | Vegetable [agrivoltaics](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics); crops between rows |
| **S2 — Functional sharing** | Ground layer is productive but subordinate to the array; grazing, forage | Solar grazing at any scale |
| **S3 — Coexistence** | *Neither sharing nor sparing.* The array takes ordinary ground outright — production stops on it — and the revenue sustains the farm enterprise that holds it. The land and the farm coexist at the level of the business rather than the field | The lease that keeps a working farm solvent and in operation |
| **S4 — Idled-land sparing** | Array occupies ground already idle, marginal, or out of production, so that productive land is spared | Awkward remnants, fallow ground, brightfields; rooftops as the limiting case |
| **S5 — Impaired-land retirement** | Production ends on ground that carried a measurable off-site burden — chronically low yields, high runoff, nutrient or pesticide export, irrigation draw beyond the aquifer's budget — or on ground positioned where that burden can be intercepted | Prairie strips on runoff-prone ground; retiring drainage-impaired irrigated fields |

**Why the centre is "neither."** Most solar on farmland is neither sharing nor sparing, and until the axis had a middle it could not say so. An ordinary array on ordinary ground produces no co-yield and retires no ground; that field becomes a power plant. But a project can restore an operation without restoring a soil: where the lease is the margin that keeps a farm from being sold — funding the succession, retiring the debt, carrying the operation through a bad decade — the project restores the enterprise even though it restores nothing in the ground. That is the [community & economic function](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community) (§4.5) doing its work. **S3 is where restoration is socioeconomic before it is biophysical.**

**S3 carries a threshold, deliberately.** Coexistence is not simply "solar on farmland." It requires that the arrangement sustain the farm enterprise holding the ground. Where the same conversion returns rent to a non-farming owner and the operation ends, that is **bare conversion** — the identical ground fact without the restorative one, and the baseline the axis is read *against* rather than a position on it. This is one of the few places the axis states a requirement instead of a description, and it is where the document's title does the work: a project that restores nothing biophysically can still be restorative if it keeps a farm farming, and a project that restores neither is a land conversion, which the lexicon can name but does not dignify with a position. Which farm, and whose, is not a rhetorical question — a lease can sustain a landowner and end a tenant's operation, so the test is read against the actors set out in §4.5.

**The positions describe the ground, not the goodness.** A position records one structural fact — what happened to production on that ground — and nothing else. Two S3 sites can differ completely: one carries gravel and herbicide, the other a native planting rich in pollinators. They occupy the same position because the ground fact is the same; they differ in the [restorative functions](4-restorative-functions.qmd) layered on them. Reading benefit off a position is the mistake §4 calls the category correction.

**Reading a site: production first, then prior status.** The positions are exclusive, and they are read in that order. If production continues within the footprint, the site is S1 or S2 — whatever the ground used to be. Only where production does *not* continue do the remaining three apply, and they are then told apart by what the ground was beforehand: ordinary (S3), already idle or marginal (S4), or carrying a measurable off-site burden (S5). A flood-prone corner that still carries the farm's sheep is S2, not S4; the same corner left to naturalize under the panels is S4. S3 additionally asks whether the farm enterprise survives the conversion; where it does not, the site is bare conversion rather than S3. This is the kind of distinction the axis exists to make quickly.

**Ecological ground layers are functions, not a position.** Pollinator habitat, prairie, and native grassland are conspicuously missing from the table above, and deliberately so: they are [restorative functions](4-restorative-functions.qmd) (§4), not positions. Those capacities are reachable from several positions at once, so giving them a position of their own would both overstate where they live and hide them everywhere else. Native grassland under a utility array is S3 carrying a biodiversity function; the same planting on retired, leaching ground is S5 carrying the same function. The axis says what happened to the production; §4 says what the land was made to do.

**S4 holds unlike things together.** Idled cropland, awkward remnants, reclaimed mine land, landfills, and brownfields share one fact — the ground was already out of production, so siting there spares land that is not — but they differ in almost everything else: prior use, contamination and hazard, permitting path, remediation constraints on foundations and ground layer, and what the community reads the reuse as meaning. The position records the shared fact; those differences belong to the site. Rooftops sit at the edge of this: a built surface spares ground completely, achieving S4's aim with no land status at all, so read it as the limiting case of the position rather than a typical member.

**The sparing wing splits on prior land status.** S4 and S5 are both removal, but they are not the same act. S4 uses ground that had already stopped paying — the array goes to the awkward corner precisely so the good field is left alone, and the sparing benefit accrues to *the land not taken*. S5 ends production on ground that was carrying a burden off-site, so it acts on *the ground taken itself* and on the water leaving it, rather than on land elsewhere. The distinction is descriptive — it names what the land was doing beforehand, not whose project is worthier — and it earns its keep at scale (§2.2), where the two behave very differently.

**Why this axis and not another.** It describes how a site is built rather than judging how it turned out, it plays no favorites, and it tells the [archetypes](6-archetypes.qmd) apart where scale alone can't. The [ecovoltaic](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-ecovoltaics) literature already reaches for land-sharing language, so this connects to an existing conversation rather than coining a private one.

### 2.2 The feasible region is a wedge, not a rectangle {#sec-wedge}

In principle the two dimensions are independent, but in practice they aren't fully — and the constraint runs through [siting latitude](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) (§1.4).

**Sparing requires the freedom to choose the ground.** Both sparing positions presuppose a designer who can select which acres to occupy. At A4–A5, where siting is governed by contiguous land assembly near a substation, that freedom is largely gone — a five-hundred-acre block will contain good and poor ground all mixed together. Large projects are therefore pushed toward the S2–S3 middle by structural necessity rather than preference: if you cannot choose *which* ground, your only remaining options are to do something worthwhile with *all* of it, or to do nothing with it at all.

**But the two sparing positions appear to fail differently at scale, and that is the point of splitting them.** The expectation — and it is an expectation, not a measured result — is that S4 thins at scale for a geometric reason: idle remnants are *scattered*, so assembling a utility project out of flood-prone corners is impractical where it is possible at all. S5 survives at scale whenever the impairment is *regional* rather than scattered — a drainage-impaired valley, a district over its groundwater budget. Where a whole landscape is impaired, retirement and scale stop fighting each other, because there is no cherry-picking to do. That asymmetry was invisible while both sat in one position.

Read the axis from its centre, which is now literally the centre: **S3 sits on the scale line**. Full and functional sharing (S1–S2) sit above it, the two removal positions (S4–S5) below. The feasible region is then not a rectangle but a **lens**: widest at A3 (Parcel) and closing toward the S2–S3 middle at both extremes of scale. It closes for different reasons at each end, and — crucially — neither end is a hard wall. Each thinned corner has a documented exception.

![The feasible region as a lens on a centred five-position axis, widest at A3 (Parcel) and closing toward the S2–S3 middle at both extremes of scale. Grazing (S2) and coexistence (S3) run the spine at every scale. Solid points are exemplar practices; hollow points are exceptions that reopen a thinned corner. Hatching marks where the space thins — lightly at small scale (feasible but atypical or negligible), densely at large scale (strongly constrained).](../figures/fig_feasible_wedge.svg){#fig-wedge}

The practical readings:

- **Grazing and coexistence are the spine.** Functional sharing (S2) is genuinely available at every scale — a farmer's own flock at A1, a contracted vegetation-management service at A3, a multi-site rotation enterprise at A5 (§1.3). Coexistence (S3) is available at every scale for the opposite reason: it asks nothing of the ground. Everything else is more scale-conditional, which is why the lens narrows around the two of them at both ends.
- **Both extremes converge on the middle.** At A5 both wings narrow: siting is dictated by assembling contiguous land, so sparing loses the freedom to choose its ground, and tight budgets make full sharing's tall clearances and wide rows hard to justify. At A1 they narrow for a gentler reason: no one farms *under* a two-panel array — they farm next to it — and a spared idle corner is real but too small to affect overall land use.
- **The thinned corners are not walls.** Each has an exception that reopens it. Small-scale full sharing returns where the structure is purpose-built to farm under — greenhouse photovoltaics. Utility-scale full sharing returns with vertical bifacial arrays, whose open inter-rows relax the clearance constraint [@vaverkova2026]. Small-scale sparing returns on rooftops: a barn roof spares ground completely, so its small footprint is the whole point rather than a limitation. Utility-scale S4 returns on uniformly low-value pre-disturbed land — reclaimed mine land, landfills, and brownfields ("brightfields") — where sparing and scale coexist without cherry-picking acres. And utility-scale S5 returns wherever impairment is regional, which is the exception with the most land behind it.
- **A3 (Parcel) is the widest part of the space.** All five positions are genuinely open at mid-scale, which is one reason Parcel-scale sites are disproportionately interesting as design exemplars.

*Native grassland is plotted at S3 because that is where it is most often built, not because it is a position; it is a [restorative function](4-restorative-functions.qmd) reachable across the axis, and at utility scale it carries documented biodiversity and soil-carbon gains [@walston2025; @krasner2025].*

**S1's appeal is not uniform across regions.** In-footprint crop benefit is strongly climate- and crop-conditional — pronounced in water-limited, high-radiation settings and for shade-tolerant crops [@barrongafford2019], but mixed to net-negative for staple grains and in temperate or humid settings where shade costs yield without a compensating water saving [@weselek2019]. Full sharing is therefore not a uniformly attractive option across the transect.

This lets the framework predict a little, not just describe — and it can be proven wrong: a utility-scale S4 project assembled from scattered marginal remnants on ordinary farmland, rather than the uniform pre-disturbed ground the exception allows, would be a real counterexample.

**It also gives the definitional dispute a home.** American Farmland Trust's position — that [dual use](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics) requires active agricultural production sustained across the project's 30–40 year life, within the array footprint — is structurally a mandate for S1–S2. Critics argue this marginalizes ecovoltaics, whose ecological ground layers deliver their value as a function rather than as production, and so sit at S3 and below. Putting both on a named axis lets the lexicon describe the disagreement precisely without adjudicating it. *(See §5, Agrivoltaics / Ecovoltaics.)*

### Associated Terminology

Terms this section introduces; cross-referenced terms link to their home section.

- **Sharing–Sparing Axis** — the second, scale-independent dimension: whether the array shares land with production, spares land by taking ground out of it, or neither. Five positions, centred on S3. Defined here.
- **S1 — Full sharing** — production continues within the array footprint, in the same ground.
- **S2 — Functional sharing** — ground layer is productive but subordinate to the array.
- **S3 — Coexistence** — neither sharing nor sparing: the array takes ordinary ground outright and the revenue sustains the farm enterprise holding it, so the restoration is socioeconomic rather than biophysical. The centre of the axis.
- **Bare conversion** — the same ground fact without the restorative one: ordinary ground converted, the operation ended. The non-restorative baseline the axis is read against, not a position on it.
- **Reading rule** — production first, then prior status: a site where production continues is S1–S2 whatever the ground used to be; only where it stops do S3–S5 apply, told apart by the ground's prior status.
- **S4 — Idled-land sparing** — array occupies ground already idle or marginal, or a built surface taking no ground at all, so productive land is spared.
- **S5 — Impaired-land retirement** — production ends on ground that carried a measurable off-site burden, or that sits where such a burden can be intercepted; the removal acts on the ground taken rather than on land elsewhere.
- **Feasible wedge** — the feasible region across scale and sharing, shaped like a lens: all five positions open at A3 (Parcel), closing toward the S2–S3 middle at both extremes — at A5 as land assembly and capital discipline remove the poles, at A1 as in-footprint farming and meaningful sparing both need more scale to be real. Grazing (S2) and coexistence (S3) are the spine; each thinned corner has an exception. Defined here (§2.2).
- **Siting latitude** — the designer's freedom over where the array goes; the constraint that makes the region a wedge. See [§1.4](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude).
- **Agrivoltaics / Ecovoltaics** — production (S1–S2) versus ecological ground layers, which are functions (§4) reachable across S2–S5. See [§5](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics).
